newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says "irrational" China may hurt HK ties.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says "irrational" China may hurt HK ties.

text.p: Taiwan pledged on Wednesday to keep business as usual with Beijing-ruled Hong Kong, but said communist China's "irrational" attitude might jeopardise the island's close economic links with the former British colony.

"Our economic and trade policy (towards Hong Kong and mainland China) can be described as forward-looking, pragmatic, and cautious," said Fu Don-cheng, economic director of the cabinet's China policy body, the Mainland Affairs Council.
"It is very flexible," Fu said at a news conference.
He said Taiwan would maintain free trade, investment and close business links with Hong Kong, but also adjust its policy to reflect evolving political reality.

Hong Kong, which returned to Beijing rule on Tuesday, is a crucial transit point for more than $30 billion in investment that has poured into China from Taiwan since the easing of unofficial ties in the late 1980s.

In its latest liberalisation, Taiwan's Finance Ministry said on Tuesday it had revised rules to allow local insurers to invest in all foreign securities, including Hong Kong's, though investment in mainland Chinese markets was still banned.
The ministry said on Wednesday the Nationalist-ruled island's banks would continue direct contacts with their Hong Kong counterparts after July 1.
Despite increasingly intricate economic ties linking Hong Kong, Taiwan and China, Taipei still bans direct investment in the mainland or official contacts there.
Council official Fu said Hong Kong was exempt -- for now.
"From July 1 onward, the status of Hong Kong has changed," Fu said. "If communist China adopts irrational policies toward Taiwan, Taiwan-Hong Kong relations will certainly be constrained."
"Cross-strait relations will have a greater impact on Taiwan-Hong Kong relations, rather then vice versa," Fu said.

Beijing, which has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since the Nationalists fled there in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war, maintains that Hong Kong's return and that of Portuguese-run Macau in 1999 will leave Taiwan as the only territory awaiting "reunification with the motherland".
Taiwan adamantly rejects union with China under the local autonomy scheme now being pioneered in Hong Kong and promoted by China's communist leaders for the long-estranged island.

"The Republic of China government (on Taiwan) will never accept such a formula," government spokesman David Lee said after mainland President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng hailed the "one country, two systems" concept as a model for Taiwan.
Taiwan Premier and Vice President Lien Chan said the people of Taiwan, now one of Asia's liveliest democracies, could never accept rule by communists.
Reunification was possible only if all China, like Taiwan itself, adopts multiparty democracy -- a scheme Lien dubbed "one country, one good system".
